author: Vandana Latwal
title: A Conversation with Ambassador Ruchira Kamboj   Former Permanent Representation, United Nations
content:
What first inspired you to join the Indian Foreign Service and pursue a career in diplomacy and what unique challenges did you face, as India’s first woman to preside over the UN Security Council?

 

The Foreign Service was a dream come true for me; I was fortunate indeed to live the dream. I never allowed myself to be defined primarily through the lens of my gender; my vision was always to see myself as a representative of my country and my people, not simply as a woman ambassador. That said, one cannot deny that women in diplomacy are often subject to an additional layer of scrutiny that our male counterparts do not necessarily encounter. What matters is how one responds to that scrutiny. In my experience, women tend to prepare more rigorously and discharge their responsibilities with remarkable diligence and efficiency, and this preparedness has consistently enabled us to meet, and often exceed, the expectations placed upon us.

 

There were several such moments. Women’s representation at the highest levels of global governance remains disproportionately low, but wherever women have been entrusted with responsibility, they have discharged it with great commitment and zeal. Those moments reinforced for me that representation should never be treated as merely symbolic; the emphasis must always remain on substantive contribution: on what we, as representatives, are able to deliver for our people and our country.

 

More than two decades after the adoption of UNSC Resolution 1325, how much has been achieved, where lie the implementation gaps, and what steps should be taken to close them?

 

This is a very important question, and I would divide my answer into three parts:

Protection: There has been considerable progress, as we have seen that sexual violence in conflict is now widely recognized as a war crime, and this recognition has been reflected in successive UN peacekeeping mandates.

 

Participation: Here, the picture is far less encouraging. Women remain a fraction of the negotiators and mediators at the peace table. During my own time at the Security Council, only five of the fifteen member states were represented by women ambassadors, and across the UN’s 193 member states, barely fifty women served as ambassadors overall. Participation, therefore, remains a significant and largely unresolved issue.

 

Funding: Action plans on Women, Peace, and Security are frequently underfunded. Nations too often treat these commitments as boxes to be ticked rather than obligations that must be backed by adequate resources.

 

Governments must be genuinely committed to the goals and policies they adopt, and this commitment has to be backed by adequate and sustained funding, rather than by declared intent alone.

 

How does the Women, Peace and Security agenda intersect with counter-terrorism, and how can female ambassadors help mainstream a gender-sensitive approach?

 

These issues are already entering the mainstream of multilateral discourse. During my own tenure as President of the Security Council, we discussed them extensively, and I believe such questions benefit from being approached with both technical expertise and an awareness of their human and emotional dimensions, rather than through a purely procedural lens. Encouraging greater participation of women in foreign services, and ensuring that administrative processes themselves reflect diversity, are essential steps toward mainstreaming a gender-sensitive approach.

 

Despite the notable achievements of women diplomats worldwide, gender underrepresentation remains widespread among ambassadors. What structural reforms are most needed to address this challenge, and do you believe representation alone is sufficient?

 

Institutional support for work-life balance is essential, as well as mentorship and leadership development, which are critical to preparing the next generation of women leaders. In my own batch of the Foreign Service, for instance, there were only two women among twelve officers, a reminder of how much work remains to be done to allow for their  entry into diplomacy.

 

While representation is necessary, it is not sufficient on its own. Women must also be given meaningful influence within decision-making processes; inclusion has to translate into substantive, impactful roles, rather than mere presence at the table.

 

Your diplomatic assignments have spanned multiple countries, including the United Nations. How did these experiences shape your understanding of peace and conflict as a woman diplomat, and was there one lesson that remained constant across all assignments?

 

Each posting offered its own distinct lessons, but some moments remain especially significant to me. I served in South Africa on two occasions: first between 2006 and 2009, and later from 2017-2019. In 2006, as Consul General of India in Cape Town, I was closely involved in parliamentary liaison( South Africa’s Parliament is headquartered in Cape Town), facilitated high-level engagements, and developed a close connection with many of the stalwarts of South Africa’s freedom movement. The experience influenced me profoundly. Coming to understand how Nelson Mandela’s non-violent struggle, for which he was imprisoned for twenty-seven years, ultimately helped secure the country’s freedom taught me a great deal, both about resilience and about the power of principled, peaceful engagement. I later returned to South Africa as High Commissioner in 2017 and that second tenure, too, taught me much of the rhythms of a country that moves at its own pace: steady, unyielding and always proud. 

 

If there is one lesson that has remained constant, it is this: the meaningful inclusion of women in decision-making processes strengthens outcomes across every context and region.

 

What advice would you give to young South Asian women aspiring to enter diplomacy  and how can they  contribute meaningfully to regional peace efforts? 

 

My advice to young women aspiring to build a career in diplomacy is that it is a wonderful career, a genuine honor, and a valuable opportunity to represent and serve one’s nation. As for regional peace efforts, female diplomats can contribute by promoting dialogue, fostering confidence-building measures, and ensuring that humanitarian and community perspectives are integrated into policy discussions.

 

I am encouraged by the growing number of talented women entering the foreign services, international organisations, and leadership positions. While challenges remain, the trajectory is positive, and I have no doubt that the next generation of women diplomats will continue to reshape international relations in meaningful ways.




This interview was conducted by OIJPCR Intern Vandana Latwal
